questions.question: Let the other players follow $\sigma_{-i}$ in an extensive-form game. When is player $i$'s strategy $\sigma_i$ sequentially rational?
options: When $\sigma_i$ is a best response to $\sigma_{-i}$ at the root, judged by her payoff over the whole game.
When, at every information set reached under $\sigma$, her continuation best responds to $\sigma_{-i}$.
When, at every information set where $i$ moves, reached or not, her continuation best responds to $\sigma_{-i}$.
When at each of her nodes she chooses the action that gives the highest payoff at the next node.

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, a player threatens to take a certain action if an opponent makes a particular move. According to sequential rationality, when is this threat credible?
options: When carrying out the threat would hurt the opponent more than it hurts the threatening player.
When the threat deters the move, so that it never has to be carried out in equilibrium.
When carrying out the threat would be optimal for her at the moment it has to be carried out.
When the threat is announced publicly before the game, so that it is common knowledge.

questions.question: Why does Nash equilibrium place no restriction on a player's action at an information set that is not reached when the equilibrium is played?
options: Unreached information sets are removed from the game before Nash equilibria are computed.
At an unreached information set the player has no actions available, so nothing can be chosen.
Nash equilibrium assumes the opponents never deviate, so unreached sets cannot ever be reached.
Changing that action leaves her payoff unchanged, so any choice there is ex-ante optimal.

questions.question: Player $i$ moves at an information set $h$ that contains several decision nodes. What is the belief $\mu(\cdot\mid h)$ used to define her sequential rationality at $h$?
options: A probability distribution over her own actions at $h$, describing how she will randomize.
A probability distribution over the terminal nodes, describing how the whole game ends.
A probability distribution over the nodes of $h$, describing where she thinks she is.
A probability that $h$ is reached at all when the strategy profile $\sigma$ is played.

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, player 1 moves at the root, player 2 then moves at a singleton node $y$, and after some of player 2's actions player 1 moves again. On what does it depend whether player 2's action at $y$ is sequentially rational?
options: Only on her payoffs at the nodes right after $y$, ignoring any later moves of player 1.
On whether $y$ is reached when the strategy profile is actually played.
On player 1's planned actions after $y$, which fix her expected payoff from $y$ on.
On nothing player 1 does, since rationality concerns only her own payoffs.

questions.question: In the entry game, the entrant chooses Out, giving $(0,2)$ to (entrant, incumbent), or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate, $(1,1)$, or Fight, $(-1,-1)$. Is the incumbent's choice of Fight sequentially rational?
options: Yes: Fight keeps the entrant out, worth $2$ to her.
Yes: her node is not reached when the entrant stays out.
No: Fight gives the entrant $-1$, less than Out's $0$.
No: at her node Accommodate gives $1>-1$.

questions.question: An incumbent sees entry but not whether the entrant is ready ($R$) or unready ($U$); both nodes form one information set, and $\mu$ is her belief that the entrant is ready. Against $R$, Fight pays her $-1$ and Accommodate $1$; against $U$, Fight pays $2$ and Accommodate $1$. With $\mu=0.2$, what is her expected payoff from Fight?

Player 1 chooses $O$ or $F$; player 2 observes this and chooses $O$ or $F$. Payoffs: $(O,O)\mapsto(2,1)$, $(F,F)\mapsto(1,2)$, $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. Player 1 plays $O$ and player 2 plays "always $F$". Is player 2's strategy sequentially rational?
options: No: after $O$ she gets $0$ from $F$ but $1$ from $O$.
Yes: "always $F$" leads to her favourite outcome $(F,F)$.
Yes: after $F$ she gets $2$, the most she can obtain.
No: after $F$ she should play $O$, which pays her more.

questions.question: In an entry game, Out gives $(0,2)$ to (entrant, incumbent). After In, Accommodate gives $(1,1)$ and Fight gives $(-1,2)$, because fighting secures the incumbent's market share. Is the incumbent's Fight sequentially rational?
options: Yes: at her node Fight gives $2>1$, so the threat is credible.
No: fighting is a threat, and threats are never credible.
No: Fight gives the entrant $-1$, which is less than $1$.
Yes, but only because the entrant then prefers to stay out.

questions.question: In the entry game, the entrant chooses Out, giving $(0,2)$ to (entrant, incumbent), or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate, $(1,1)$, or Fight, $(-1,-1)$. Suppose the entrant plays Out. In the normal-form sense, which of the incumbent's strategies are best responses to Out?
options: Only Accommodate, since it gives her $1>-1$ after In.
Only Fight, since it is what keeps the entrant out.
Both Accommodate and Fight, since each gives her $2$ against Out.
Neither, since she does not move when the entrant plays Out.

questions.question: Player 1's plan avoids one of her own later information sets, so that set is never reached. Why does sequential rationality still require her action there to be optimal?
options: Because her payoff in the play that occurs would change if the action at that set were changed.
Others' optimal replies and her own earlier choice depend on what she would do there.
Because a strategy only needs to list actions at sets that its own earlier moves leave reachable.
Because otherwise the game would not have perfect information at the set that is never reached.

questions.question: An incumbent sees entry but not whether the entrant is ready ($R$) or unready ($U$); both nodes form one information set, and $\mu$ is her belief that the entrant is ready. Against $R$, Fight pays $-1$ and Accommodate $1$; against $U$, Fight pays $2$ and Accommodate $1$. At $\mu=\tfrac{1}{3}$, which statement about her sequentially rational actions is correct?
options: Both actions are sequentially rational, as both give expected payoff $1$.
Neither action is sequentially rational, as no action is strictly better.
Only Accommodate, since a tie must be broken in favour of the safe action.
Only Fight, since Fight is better against $U$, the more likely node.

questions.question: In a trust game, player 1 chooses Keep, giving $(1,1)$, or Trust; after Trust, player 2 chooses Share, $(2,2)$, or Grab, $(0,3)$. Player 2 promises to Share if trusted. Is this promise credible in the sense of sequential rationality?
options: Yes: sharing gives both players more than Keep.
Yes: credibility only matters for threats.
No: Share gives player 1 more than Grab.
No: once trusted, Grab gives player 2 $3>2$.

questions.question: An incumbent sees entry but not whether the entrant is ready ($R$) or unready ($U$); both nodes form one information set, and $\mu$ is her belief that the entrant is ready. Against $R$, Fight pays her $-2$ and Accommodate $1$; against $U$, Fight pays $3$ and Accommodate $1$. For which beliefs $\mu$ is Fight sequentially rational?
options: $\mu\ge\tfrac{2}{5}$
$\mu\le\tfrac{1}{3}$
$\mu\ge\tfrac{3}{5}$
$\mu\le\tfrac{2}{5}$

questions.question: Player 1 chooses Stop, $(1,0)$, or Continue; player 2 then chooses Stop, $(0,2)$, or Continue; player 1 then chooses Stop, $(3,1)$, or Continue, $(2,4)$. Player 1's strategy is (Stop at the first node, Continue at the last). Is it sequentially rational?
options: Yes: her last node is never reached, so any action there is acceptable.
No: at her last node Stop gives $3>2$, even though that node is never reached.
Yes: Stop at the first node secures $1$, which is all that is required.
No: at her first node Continue gives her $3$, which is more than $1$.

questions.question: In the entry game, the entrant chooses Out, giving $(0,2)$ to (entrant, incumbent), or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate, $(1,1)$, or Fight, $(-1,-1)$. The entrant plays In with probability $0.1$ and Out with probability $0.9$. Is Fight a best response of the incumbent to this strategy?
options: No: her node is reached with positive probability, and there $1>-1$.
Yes: against Out she gets $2$ either way, and Out is far more likely.
Yes: with entry only $0.1$ likely, her choice there hardly matters.
No: Fight gives the entrant an expected payoff below $0$.

questions.question: In a Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game with singleton information sets, suppose every information set is reached with positive probability. What follows about sequential rationality?
options: Nothing: Nash equilibrium never implies optimality at any information set after the root.
Every player's strategy is optimal at every information set, so it is sequentially rational.
Only the first mover is sequentially rational; later movers may still choose suboptimally.
Sequential rationality fails, since mixing is never optimal at a single information set.

questions.question: In an entry game, Out gives $(0,2)$ to (entrant, incumbent); after In, Accommodate gives $(1,0)$ and Fight gives $(-1,0)$. Is the profile (Out, Fight) sequentially rational for both players?
options: No: Fight is a threat that is never carried out, so it cannot be credible.
No: Accommodate gives the entrant $1$, so the incumbent must accommodate.
Yes, but only because the incumbent's node is never reached under Out.
Yes: the incumbent is indifferent at her node, and given Fight, Out ($0>-1$) is optimal.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses Stop, $(2,0)$, or Go. After Go, player 2 chooses $l$, $(1,1)$, or $r$. After $r$, player 1 chooses $a$, $(0,3)$, or $b$, $(3,0)$. Which profile is sequentially rational at every node?
options: Player 1: Stop and $b$; player 2: $r$.
Player 1: Stop and $b$; player 2: $l$.
Player 1: Go and $b$; player 2: $l$.
Player 1: Stop and $a$; player 2: $l$.

questions.question: An incumbent sees entry but not whether the entrant is ready ($R$) or unready ($U$); both nodes form one information set, and $\mu$ is her belief that the entrant is ready. She can Fight, Accommodate or Share. Against $R$: Fight $-1$, Accommodate $1$, Share $0$. Against $U$: Fight $2$, Accommodate $0$, Share $1.5$. For which beliefs $\mu$ is Share sequentially rational?
options: $\tfrac{1}{3}\le\mu\le\tfrac{3}{5}$
For no $\mu$ at all
$\mu\le\tfrac{1}{3}$
$\mu\ge\tfrac{3}{5}$
